#1 Not long ago, it was suggested by eminent membrane biologists that there is no unifying model of membrane structure (https://doi.org/10.3389/fcell.2016.00106; https://doi.org/10.3390/biomedicines10071711). This is partially due to membrane biology being overrun by the lipid raft theory, a pseudoscience that survives by shifting its definitions in response to contradictory evidence (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/397646378_Lessons_from_pseudoscience_in_biology). To address the "no model" and lipid raft problems, two years ago we published the proteolipid code; a snarky proposition that gains falsifiability by contradicting claims made by lipid raft loyalists (https://doi.org/10.1186/s12915-024-01849-6; https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17201252).

I was trained as a membrane protein biochemist and structural biologist, however I recently abandoned experiments to continue developing the PL code theoretically. This includes learning a small amount of category theory to write this very modest paper, which I humbly share with you who have more experience in the area:

Kervin, T.A. Sheaf-theoretic representation of the proteolipid code. arXiv preprint arXiv:2512.23784 (2025). https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2512.23784

Although poorly written and amateurish, I hope this might on the off chance inspire some physicists and applied category theorists to inspect, and maybe even develop an interest in, the fascinating thing that I am trying to represent: a code that is much larger than the genetic code in terms of mass, volume, and number of components, yet has been overlooked until now.
subject: Sheaf-theoretic representation of the proteolipid code
